PERSISTENCE BEYOND POWER-OFF
Variables in RAM vanish the millisecond the program exits or the machine powers down. Files bridge volatile RAM to non-volatile disk storage.
ALGORITHMIC MASTERY
Searching and sorting form 80% of all computational tasks. Understanding asymptotic limits ($O(n)$ vs $O(n^2)$ vs $O(n log n)$) separates amateur coders from systems engineers.
01 · file fundamentals

STREAMS & FILE POINTERS — THE FILE STRUCTURE

files_sort_003.c
/* Standard Streams pre-opened by runtime:
   stdin  (Keyboard, file descriptor 0)
   stdout (Terminal screen, fd 1)
   stderr (Terminal unbuffered error stream, fd 2) */

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    /* FILE is an opaque typedef struct managing
       stream state, buffers, error flags, and cursor */
    FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        perror("Failed to open data.txt");
        return 1;
    }
    printf("File opened successfully!\n");
    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}
THE FILE * HANDLE
You never access FILE struct members directly. You pass the opaque FILE* pointer to standard library stream functions.
STREAM ABSTRACTION
Treats files on SSD, keyboard keystrokes, and network sockets as uniform linear byte streams.
02 · file modes

FOPEN & FILE MODES — READ, WRITE & APPEND

files_sort_004.c
/* TEXT MODES:
   "r"  - Read text. File MUST exist!
   "w"  - Write text. Creates new or TRUNCATES existing!
   "a"  - Append text. Creates new or appends to end.
   "r+" - Read & Write. File must exist.
   "w+" - Read & Write. Truncates existing file!
   "a+" - Read & Append. Preserves existing content.

   BINARY MODES:
   "rb", "wb", "ab", "r+b", "w+b", "a+b"
   Always add 'b' on Windows to prevent CRLF conversions! */
TRUNCATION DANGER
Opening with "w" instantly wipes out the existing file contents without asking! Double check mode string.
MANDATORY NULL CHECK
fopen returns NULL if the file does not exist, disk is full, or permissions are denied. Always check fp == NULL!
03 · character file I/O

CHARACTER I/O (FGETC / FPUTC) — FILE COPY UTILITY

files_sort_005.c
#include <stdio.h>

int copy_file(const char *src, const char *dst) {
    FILE *in  = fopen(src, "rb");
    FILE *out = fopen(dst, "wb");
    if (!in || !out) { if(in) fclose(in); return 0; }

    int ch; /* MUST be int to accommodate EOF (-1)! */
    while ((ch = fgetc(in)) != EOF) {
        fputc(ch, out);
    }

    fclose(in);
    fclose(out);
    return 1; /* Success */
}
WHY ch IS int
fgetc returns an unsigned char promoted to int, or negative EOF (-1) on end-of-file. If ch is char, byte 0xFF might falsely trigger EOF!
STREAM CLOSING
fclose flushes any buffered bytes to disk and releases OS kernel file descriptors. Always close files.
04 · line file I/O

LINE I/O (FGETS & FPUTS) — SAFE TEXT PROCESSING

files_sort_006.c
#include <stdio.h>

void display_file(const char *filename) {
    FILE *fp = fopen(filename, "r");
    if (!fp) return;

    char line_buf[256];
    int line_no = 1;

    /* fgets returns NULL when EOF is reached */
    while (fgets(line_buf, sizeof(line_buf), fp) != NULL) {
        printf("%03d: %s", line_no++, line_buf);
    }
    fclose(fp);
}
SAFE BUFFER LIMITS
fgets reads up to size-1 characters or stops at newline \n, guaranteeing zero buffer overflows.
LINE NUMBERING
Foundation of command-line tools like grep, cat -n, and compiler source diagnostic printouts.
05 · formatted file I/O

FORMATTED FILE I/O — FPRINTF & FSCANF

files_sort_007.c
typedef struct { int id; char name[20]; double gpa; } rec_t;

/* Write formatted record */
void save_record(FILE *fp, const rec_t *r) {
    fprintf(fp, "%d %s %.2f\n", r->id, r->name, r->gpa);
}

/* Read formatted record */
int load_record(FILE *fp, rec_t *r) {
    /* fscanf returns count of successfully matched items */
    return (fscanf(fp, "%d %s %lf",
                   &r->id, r->name, &r->gpa) == 3);
}
FPRINTF FLEXIBILITY
Mirrors printf, but writes output to the specified stream pointer instead of the console terminal.
RETURN VALUE CHECKING
Always verify fscanf return value equals the expected token count (here 3). Anything less means corrupt data or EOF.
06 · binary files

BINARY FILES (FWRITE / FREAD) — RAW MEMORY SERIALIZATION

files_sort_008.c
typedef struct { int acc_no; double balance; } acc_t;

void save_account(FILE *fp, const acc_t *acc) {
    /* Writes raw memory image directly to disk! */
    fwrite(acc, sizeof(acc_t), 1, fp);
}

int load_account(FILE *fp, acc_t *acc) {
    /* Reads raw memory block directly from disk */
    return (fread(acc, sizeof(acc_t), 1, fp) == 1);
}
WHY BINARY IS 10x FASTER
Bypasses string formatting and ASCII text conversions. Directly dumps and reads RAM memory blocks to disk.
EXACT PRECISION
Floating-point values (IEEE 754) retain their exact bit-for-bit precision without rounding errors caused by %f conversions.
07 · random access

RANDOM ACCESS (fseek & ftell) — O(1) DISK INDEXING

files_sort_009.c
#include <stdio.h>

/* whence options:
   SEEK_SET - Offset from beginning of file
   SEEK_CUR - Offset from current cursor position
   SEEK_END - Offset from end of file */

long get_file_size(FILE *fp) {
    fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END); /* Jump to end */
    long size = ftell(fp);  /* Read byte offset */
    rewind(fp);             /* Reset cursor to start */
    return size;
}
DIRECT SEEKING
fseek jumps the stream cursor to any arbitrary byte in O(1) time without reading through preceding bytes.
ftell() POSITION
Returns the current byte offset from the start of the file. Essential for file size calculation and record checkpointing.
08 · in-place record updates

IN-PLACE RECORD UPDATES — DIRECT DATABASE MODIFICATION

files_sort_010.c
void update_balance(FILE *fp, int record_index, double new_bal) {
    acc_t acc;
    long offset = record_index * sizeof(acc_t);

    /* 1. Seek directly to record */
    fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET);

    /* 2. Read existing */
    fread(&acc, sizeof(acc_t), 1, fp);
    acc.balance = new_bal;

    /* 3. Seek BACK to same position and rewrite */
    fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET);
    fwrite(&acc, sizeof(acc_t), 1, fp);
}
R+B MODE
Opening with "r+b" enables read and write simultaneously on binary files without truncating.
ZERO REWRITE OVERHEAD
Modifies record #50,000 instantly without having to read or re-write the other 49,999 records!
09 · database searching

SEARCHING A DATABASE ON FILES — SEQUENTIAL vs DISK BINARY SEARCH

files_sort_011.c
int find_account_by_id(FILE *fp, int target_id, acc_t *result) {
    rewind(fp);
    acc_t temp;
    while (fread(&temp, sizeof(acc_t), 1, fp) == 1) {
        if (temp.acc_no == target_id) {
            *result = temp;
            return 1; /* Found! */
        }
    }
    return 0; /* Not found */
}
DISK SCAN
Sequential scan reads records sequentially until matching ID is found. O(n) disk reads.
INDEXED ACCESS
If files are maintained in sorted order by ID, disk binary search using fseek can locate any record in O(log n) seeks!
10 · linear search depth

LINEAR SEARCH IN DEPTH — ALGORITHM & COMPLEXITY

files_sort_012.c
/* Comprehensive Linear Search */
int linear_search(const int arr[], int n, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) return i; /* O(1) best case */
    }
    return -1; /* O(n) worst case */
}

/* Sentinel Optimization (Removes bounds check in inner loop) */
int sentinel_search(int a[], int n, int target) {
    int last = a[n - 1]; a[n - 1] = target;
    int i = 0; while (a[i] != target) i++;
    a[n - 1] = last;
    return (i < n - 1 || last == target) ? i : -1;
}
APPLICABILITY
Works on ANY array: unsorted, linked lists, files. Zero prerequisites.
COMPLEXITY
Best Case: O(1) (found at index 0). Worst Case: O(n) (absent or last). Average: O(n/2) comparisons.
11 · binary search depth

BINARY SEARCH IN DEPTH — O(log n) LOGARITHMIC SCALING

files_sort_013.c
int binary_search(const int a[], int n, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = n - 1;

    while (lo <= hi) {
        /* Prevents integer overflow: lo + (hi - lo)/2 */
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

        if (a[mid] == target)      return mid;      /* Found */
        else if (a[mid] < target)  lo = mid + 1;    /* Right */
        else                       hi = mid - 1;    /* Left */
    }
    return -1; /* Not found */
}
PREREQUISITE
Array MUST BE SORTED. If unsorted, binary search produces incorrect results.
LOGARITHMIC POWER
Searching 1,000,000,000 (one billion) elements requires at most 30 comparisons! log2(10^9) ≈ 30.
12 · bubble sort depth

BUBBLE SORT IN DEPTH — PASS TRACE & SWAPPED FLAG

files_sort_014.c
void bubble_sort(int a[], int n) {
    for (int pass = 0; pass < n - 1; pass++) {
        int swapped = 0; /* Early exit flag */
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 1 - pass; i++) {
            if (a[i] > a[i + 1]) {
                int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[i + 1]; a[i + 1] = t;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }
        /* If no swaps occurred, array is ALREADY sorted! */
        if (!swapped) break;
    }
}
SWAPPED OPTIMIZATION
Reduces best case to O(n) on already-sorted arrays. Exits on pass 1.
STABILITY
Bubble sort is STABLE: equal keys retain their original relative order because strict > comparison never swaps equals.
13 · selection sort depth

SELECTION SORT IN DEPTH — MINIMAL MEMORY WRITES

files_sort_015.c
void selection_sort(int a[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int min_idx = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (a[j] < a[min_idx]) min_idx = j;
        }
        /* Swap only ONCE per pass */
        if (min_idx != i) {
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[min_idx]; a[min_idx] = t;
        }
    }
}
MINIMAL SWAPS
Performs at most n-1 swaps across the entire sort. Excellent for EEPROM / Flash memory where writes are expensive.
NOT STABLE
Long-distance swaps can reorder identical elements. Time complexity is O(n^2) in all cases (best, avg, worst).
14 · insertion sort depth

INSERTION SORT IN DEPTH — ADAPTIVE & ONLINE

files_sort_016.c
void insertion_sort(int a[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int key = a[i];
        int j = i - 1;

        /* Shift elements greater than key to the right */
        while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {
            a[j + 1] = a[j];
            j--;
        }
        a[j + 1] = key; /* Insert into correct position */
    }
}
CARD PLAYER ANALOGY
Picks up next card and slides it into its proper sorted position among already-sorted cards on the left.
ADAPTIVE & ONLINE
Runs in O(n) linear time on nearly-sorted data. Can sort data as it arrives in real time (online algorithm).
15 · algorithm comparison

THE COMPLEXITY SHOWDOWN — TIME, SPACE & STABILITY

files_sort_017.c
/* ALGORITHM SHOWDOWN MATRIX:
   Algorithm   | Best    | Average | Worst   | Space | Stable?
   -------------------------------------------------------
   Linear Srch | O(1)    | O(n/2)  | O(n)    | O(1)  | Yes
   Binary Srch | O(1)    | O(logn) | O(logn) | O(1)  | Yes
   Bubble Sort | O(n)*   | O(n^2)  | O(n^2)  | O(1)  | Yes
   Select Sort | O(n^2)  | O(n^2)  | O(n^2)  | O(1)  | No
   Insert Sort | O(n)    | O(n^2)  | O(n^2)  | O(1)  | Yes
   qsort()     | O(nlogn)| O(nlogn)| O(n^2)  | O(logn)| No
   *with swapped flag */
ASYMPTOTIC TRUTH
For small N (under 20), Insertion Sort is often faster than Quicksort due to low constant overhead.
PRODUCTION CHOICE
For general in-memory sorting of large datasets, always use standard library qsort() from .
16 · standard library qsort

STDLIB QSORT & BSEARCH — GENERIC VOID* POLYMORPHISM

files_sort_018.c
#include <stdlib.h>

int compare_ints(const void *a, const void *b) {
    int arg1 = *(const int*)a;
    int arg2 = *(const int*)b;
    return (arg1 > arg2) - (arg1 < arg2);
}

int main(void) {
    int arr[] = {64, 25, 12, 22, 11};
    int n = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);

    qsort(arr, n, sizeof(int), compare_ints);
    /* arr is now sorted: 11, 12, 22, 25, 64 */

    int key = 22;
    int *found = (int*)bsearch(&key, arr, n, sizeof(int), compare_ints);
    if (found) printf("Found %d at index %ld\n", key, found - arr);
    return 0;
}
GENERIC C
qsort and bsearch sort and search ANY data type by using void* pointers and custom comparator callbacks.
COMPARATOR CONTRACT
Return < 0 if a comes first, 0 if equal, > 0 if b comes first.
17 · command-line arguments

COMMAND LINE ARGUMENTS — ARGC & ARGV

files_sort_019.c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    printf("Program executable: %s\n", argv[0]);
    printf("Total arguments passed: %d\n", argc);

    for (int i = 1; i < argc; i++) {
        printf("Argument %d: '%s'\n", i, argv[i]);
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Running: $ ./app -v input.txt 100
   argc = 4, argv[0]="./app", argv[1]="-v", argv[2]="input.txt" */
argc (COUNT)
Integer count of tokens typed in shell. Always >= 1 because argv[0] contains program name.
argv (VECTOR)
Array of pointers to strings: char *argv[]. Null-terminated character arrays.
unit V · atom 20

FEOF vs FERROR STREAM STATUS INSPECTION

files_sort_020.c
int ch = fgetc(fp);
if (ch == EOF) {
    if (feof(fp))   printf("Reached clean end of file\n");
    if (ferror(fp)) perror("Hardware stream read error!");
}
NEVER while(!feof)
feof() returns true ONLY AFTER an attempted read hits EOF. Checking before reading causes duplicate last items!
CLEARERR
clearerr(fp) resets error and end-of-file indicators on the stream.
unit V · atom 21

REWINDING STREAMS RESETTING POSITION

files_sort_021.c
rewind(fp); /* Equivalent to fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) */
clearerr(fp); /* Also clears error flags! */
CONVENIENCE IDIOM
rewind(fp) resets the stream pointer back to byte 0 and clears error flags.
TWO-PASS PROCESSING
Used when first pass counts records and second pass loads them into memory.
unit V · atom 22

ALGORITHM STABILITY PRESERVING RELATIVE ORDER

files_sort_022.c
/* Consider records: [Alice(90), Bob(85), Charlie(90)]
   Stable Sort preserves Alice before Charlie:
   -> [Bob(85), Alice(90), Charlie(90)] ✓
   Unstable Sort may invert their order:
   -> [Bob(85), Charlie(90), Alice(90)] ✗ */
WHY STABILITY MATTERS
When sorting multi-column tables (e.g. sort by Name, then sort by Department), stability guarantees previous sort order is not corrupted.
STABLE SORTS
Bubble Sort, Insertion Sort, and Merge Sort are stable. Selection Sort and Quicksort are unstable.
unit V · atom 23

BIG-O, OMEGA & THETA FORMAL BOUNDS

files_sort_023.c
/* Big-O (O):      Upper bound (Worst case guarantee)
   Big-Omega (Ω):  Lower bound (Best case potential)
   Big-Theta (Θ):  Tight bound (Upper AND Lower match) */
// Example: Selection Sort is Θ(n^2) in all cases!
ASYMPTOTIC METRICS
Measures algorithm scaling as input size N tends toward infinity, ignoring constant hardware factors.
SYSTEM DESIGN
Engineers design systems around worst-case Big-O bounds to guarantee predictable latency under heavy loads.

/* Consider records: [Alice(90), Bob(85), Charlie(90)]
   Stable Sort preserves Alice before Charlie:
   -> [Bob(85), Alice(90), Charlie(90)] ✓
   Unstable Sort may invert their order:
   -> [Bob(85), Charlie(90), Alice(90)] ✗ */
WHY STABILITY MATTERS
When sorting multi-column tables (e.g. sort by Name, then sort by Department), stability guarantees previous sort order is not corrupted.
STABLE SORTS
Bubble Sort, Insertion Sort, and Merge Sort are stable. Selection Sort and Quicksort are unstable.

BIG-O, OMEGA & THETA · DRILL 14 FORMAL BOUNDS

files_sort_088.c
/* Big-O (O):      Upper bound (Worst case guarantee)
   Big-Omega (Ω):  Lower bound (Best case potential)
   Big-Theta (Θ):  Tight bound (Upper AND Lower match) */
// Example: Selection Sort is Θ(n^2) in all cases!
ASYMPTOTIC METRICS
Measures algorithm scaling as input size N tends toward infinity, ignoring constant hardware factors.
SYSTEM DESIGN
Engineers design systems around worst-case Big-O bounds to guarantee predictable latency under heavy loads.

INDEX FILE PATTERN · DRILL 14 IN-MEMORY FAST KEYS

files_sort_089.c
typedef struct { int key; long file_offset; } index_entry_t;

index_entry_t index_table[1000];
// Binary search in-memory index table in O(log n),
// then single fseek() directly to disk offset!
INDEX ACCELERATION
Keeps small compact index table in RAM. Performs binary search in RAM, requiring only 1 disk seek to read full record.
DATABASE ARCHITECTURE
Foundation of B-Trees, SQLite, PostgreSQL, and modern enterprise database indexing engines.
unit V · atom 90

FEOF vs FERROR · DRILL 15 STREAM STATUS INSPECTION

files_sort_090.c
int ch = fgetc(fp);
if (ch == EOF) {
    if (feof(fp))   printf("Reached clean end of file\n");
    if (ferror(fp)) perror("Hardware stream read error!");
}
NEVER while(!feof)
feof() returns true ONLY AFTER an attempted read hits EOF. Checking before reading causes duplicate last items!
CLEARERR
clearerr(fp) resets error and end-of-file indicators on the stream.
unit V · atom 91

REWINDING STREAMS · DRILL 15 RESETTING POSITION

files_sort_091.c
rewind(fp); /* Equivalent to fseek(fp, 0L, SEEK_SET) */
clearerr(fp); /* Also clears error flags! */
CONVENIENCE IDIOM
rewind(fp) resets the stream pointer back to byte 0 and clears error flags.
TWO-PASS PROCESSING
Used when first pass counts records and second pass loads them into memory.
